title: How to Conjugate Re Verbs in French the Right Way
summary: You can recite the endings chart and still freeze when a native speaker uses vendre mid-sentence. Here is why that happens, and how to fix it for good.Learners…
body_markdown:
**You can recite the endings chart and still freeze when a native speaker uses vendre mid-sentence. Here is why that happens, and how to fix it for good.**


Learners who struggle with *RE verb conjugation* are not struggling because they skipped the chart. The common assumption is that if you just memorize the endings chart well enough, you will be able to use RE verbs automatically in conversation. Most have stared at it.


They can recite "je vends, tu vends, il vend" in order, pass a fill-in-the-blank worksheet, and still freeze the moment a native speaker says "il vend" in a real sentence. That freeze is not a motivation problem. It is a structural one, built into how French grammar is taught from the start.


See our[learn Spanish](https://www.parrotapp.com/) for how this works in practice. According to industry research, instructional materials and classroom time are heavily skewed toward -ER verbs, leaving the -RE family systematically under-practised. Learners build confidence with parler and aimer, then hit vendre and attendre with almost no preparation.


Less exposure means fewer chances for the pattern to become automatic. Fewer chances means the form stays fragile under pressure. The stem stands bare.


A learner who has internalized the -ER logic ("always add something") expects "il vende" and produces exactly that. The zero-ending rule is a well-documented source of learner error, routinely buried in conjugation charts rather than called out as the exception it is. The chart shows the blank cell.


It rarely explains why the cell is blank, or why that silence sounds so wrong to a learner trained on -ER endings. Knowing a rule and hearing it in real time are two different cognitive tasks. The pattern only becomes automatic when the brain processes it in context, not in isolation.


Before you can fix the problem, you need a clear picture of what -RE verbs actually are and why their stem-plus-ending logic is simpler, and more consistent, than most courses make it look.


*Knowing a rule and hearing it in real time are two different cognitive tasks.*


## Key takeaways


-


Regular -RE verbs follow one formula: drop the infinitive ending, then add -s, -s, -, -ons, -ez, -ent, every present-tense form unlocks from that single stem.


-


Passé composé with -RE verbs freezes learners mid-story not because they forgot the rule, but because most courses teach past tenses weeks apart, so retrieval collapses when both are needed in the same sentence.


-


Future and conditional share one stem for -RE verbs, vendrai versus vendrais is the only variable, which means treating them as two separate memorization tasks doubles the work for no reason.


-


High-frequency irregular -RE verbs like prendre break the standard stem-plus-ending formula entirely, so false confidence from the regular chart is one of the fastest ways to stall at an intermediate plateau.


-


Acing a conjugation worksheet and handling live French speech run on different cognitive systems, neurolinguistic research distinguishes explicit rule recall from the automatic pattern retrieval fluency actually requires.


-


Parrot closes that gap by delivering short-form French video built on comprehensible input, the most researched method for acquisition, so -RE verb patterns move from rules you remember to sounds you recognize at full conversational speed.


## What Makes RE Verbs a Distinct Pattern Worth Understanding Fully


Three[verb families](https://www.mattfrenchtutor.com/courses/conjugation-lessons/french-verbs-groups/) exist in French, but most learners spend the vast majority of their time on one. The *-ER* family dominates beginner textbooks, *-IR* verbs get a respectful chapter, and *-RE* verbs are handed over in a single crowded table with no explanation of what makes them structurally different. Whether *-RE* verbs count as "regular" or "irregular" depends entirely on the teaching framework being used.


Native French schooling categorizes them differently from FSL (French as a Second Language) curricula, so a learner who switches resources mid-journey often finds the same verb labeled both ways. French groups its verbs by infinitive ending, and Fluent French Now identifies the three families as *-ER* , *-IR* , and *-RE* , each with its own ending logic. The structural reason *-RE* verbs form a separate category comes down to one defining feature: the[third-person singular](https://www.lawlessfrench.com/grammar/pronouns-and-adjectives-3s/) takes no added ending at all.


Compare the three families side by side and the contrast is immediate.


-


**il/elle** → **-ER (parler):** parl **e** → **-IR (finir):** fin **it** → **-RE (vendre):** vend (bare stem).


Where *-ER* adds an *-e* and *-IR* adds a *-t* , the *-RE* verb stops at the stem. That zero-ending rule,[documented in research on French](http://www.glendon.yorku.ca/rmougeon/website(publish) subject-verb agreement by Nadasdi at Glendon College/nadracla.htm), reflects a broader feature of spoken French where[third-person singular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_conjugation) and plural forms are often phonetically identical. This is precisely why the pattern that looks obvious on paper disappears in the ear: the stem-final consonant is what separates "il vend" from silence, and you only train that ear by absorbing it from native-level speech, not from a conjugation table.


### The One-Step Stem Rule That Makes Every Regular RE Verb Predictable


The stem rule is mechanical. Fluent French Now states it plainly: drop *-re* from the infinitive, and what remains is the stem. *Vendre* becomes *vend-* .


*Attendre* becomes *attend-* . *Perdre* becomes *perd-* . Every regular *-RE* verb follows this same one-step process, which means learning the rule once unlocks the entire family rather than one verb at a time.


That stem is the foundation every tense builds on: present tense,[passé composé](https://www.frenchtoday.com/blog/french-verb-conjugation/passe-compose/) , imparfait, future, all start from the same stripped stem. The vocabulary and natural speech patterns that make *-RE* verbs feel automatic come from repeated exposure to native-level content, the kind of input where "il attend" and "ils attendent" are heard in context, not studied in isolation. Not all *-RE* verbs earn equal attention.


Fluent French Now identifies seven regular *-RE* verbs that appear constantly in real French: **vendre** (to sell), attendre (to wait), perdre (to lose), répondre (to answer), rendre (to return or give back), entendre (to hear), and descendre (to go down). The most efficient path to internalizing these seven is hearing them in authentic speech before being asked to produce them. When a learner is ready to move from recognition to production, the Parrot Back speaking practice feature creates a loop, hear it, then say it back, that converts passive familiarity into active control.


## How to Conjugate Regular RE Verbs in the Present Tense Without Blanking Mid-Sentence


Every[present-tense form](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESqAEB6zswFca-YaJFCUxhkiwk4G1mFkqSNWGCsJu94T1tNqY0-PC_h8zieciSbLjG48jnJPd3JcD6Rc9b_fjI14XevDReyATynRfhey1ppe11NXkWDgDFrG8Moh5978vA-b6QeCPM0L51AtBZFYbDebTA1o8S82sJGHc5H8rr4PaWugmSoY97B8yDypU8sCoowMztYiFGOeBlLo1r7A1cfkqYCd6AUpOt1Zs) of every regular -RE verb in French unlocks from that single formula. The table itself is easy to memorize, but as[Poiret and Liu found](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-french-language-studies/article/some-quantitative-aspects-of-written-and-spoken-french-based-on-syntactically-annotated-corpora/0B6C5B319507A0E3D495BFF18649A889) in the Journal of French Language Studies, exposure to a written conjugation chart does not automatically transfer to spoken production, because written and spoken French distribute their verb forms very differently. Knowing the procedure is therefore the essential first step.


Strip *-re* from the infinitive. What remains is the stem, and the endings in the table below attach directly to it.


-


**je** → **Ending:** -s → **Example:** je vends.


-


**tu** → **Ending:** -s → **Example:** tu vends.


-


**il/elle/on** → **Ending:** (nothing) → **Example:** il vend.


-


**nous** → **Ending:** -ons → **Example:** nous vendons.


-


**vous** → **Ending:** -ez → **Example:** vous vendez.


-


**ils/elles** → **Ending:** -ent → **Example:** ils vendent.


Notice that the il/elle/on row carries no ending whatsoever. That fact surprises almost every learner who first encounters it, and it matters more than any other slot in the table.


### The Silent Third-Person Trap - Why Il/Elle/On Gets No Ending at All


It is the rule. For regular -RE verbs, the third-person singular form is simply the bare stem: *vend* , *répond* , *attend* . Understanding why that zero ending causes real difficulty requires looking at how spoken French actually works.


Here is why this creates real problems in conversation.[Poiret and Liu's corpus research](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-french-language-studies/article/some-quantitative-aspects-of-written-and-spoken-french-based-on-syntactically-annotated-corpora/0B6C5B319507A0E3D495BFF18649A889) shows that spoken French is dominated by pronoun subjects, meaning *il* , *elle* , and *on* appear far more often in real speech than a written chart would suggest. The form your chart most easily obscures is the one native speakers use most.


Worth noting: the *-ent* ending on *ils/elles* is also completely silent. *Ils vendent* and *il vend* sound identical. The only signal is the subject pronoun itself, which reinforces why training your ear to the pronoun, not the ending, is the key skill to develop.


This is a struggle that hits learners hard precisely because verb conjugation is so often presented in fragments, a table here, a rule there, rather than in logically organized blocks tied to how the language actually sounds. When the pattern is not wired to real spoken input, gaps, hesitations, and mid-sentence insecurities follow.


### Vendre in Full - Every Form Anchored to a Real Sentence


The most effective way to internalize the pattern is to see each form inside a sentence you would actually say. Here is every present-tense form paired with a sentence you would actually hear:


-


**Je vends** mon vélo. (I'm selling my bike.)


-


**Tu vends** des billets? (Are you selling tickets?)


-


**Il vend sa voiture ce week-end.** (He's selling his car this weekend.)


-


**Nous vendons** tout en ligne. (We sell everything online.)


-


**Vous vendez** ça ici? (Do you sell that here?)


-


**Ils vendent** au marché. (They sell at the market.)


Notice that *il vend* carries no added sound. Say it aloud: the *d* is silent in natural speech, making the pronoun the only reliable cue.


*Répondre* (to answer) follows the identical procedure, and working through it cements the pattern across a second verb.


Hearing these forms spoken by real French voices in context is what shifts them from chart-recognition to automatic retrieval, and that shift is precisely what traditional memorization-based approaches fail to produce.[Poiret and Liu's corpus findings](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-french-language-studies/article/some-quantitative-aspects-of-written-and-spoken-french-based-on-syntactically-annotated-corpora/0B6C5B319507A0E3D495BFF18649A889) make clear that the distribution of verb forms in authentic spoken French looks nothing like the even spread a textbook table implies. Short, repeated exposure to real spoken French, the kind that lets you hear *il vend* and *ils vendent* in natural context rather than in isolation, wires the -RE verb pattern to sound rather than to a static grid. You now have the present-tense pattern locked in with two model verbs, *vendre* and *répondre* , and real sentences to anchor each form.


## How to Form the Passé Composé With RE Verbs So the Past Tense Finally Sticks


Choosing the wrong past tense mid-story is a retrieval problem, and it hits hardest with RE verbs because most learners[study the passé composé](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8759977/) and imparfait in separate units, weeks apart, and then wonder why they freeze when both tenses are needed in the same breath. Alliance Française Vancouver makes the semantic boundary explicit: the passé composé marks a completed action with a defined endpoint, while the imparfait covers ongoing or habitual past states. Learning them side by side closes that gap, and that is exactly where traditional memorization-based methods tend to fail beginners who need the contrast to feel intuitive before it can be deployed under real conversational pressure.


### The One Past-Participle Rule That Covers Every Regular RE Verb


Forming the past participle of any regular RE verb requires only one step: drop the infinitive ending and add *u* . Vendre becomes vendu, perdre becomes perdu, and attendre becomes attendu, the same mechanical swap every time. For the auxiliary, Lawless French confirms that regular RE verbs take *avoir* , not être, with regular RE verbs, avoir is the default every time. With avoir verbs, the past participle does not agree with the subject, so vendu stays vendu regardless of who is doing the selling, unless a direct-object pronoun precedes the verb, as in *je l'ai vendu* , in which case agreement applies. " *(Here,* l'* is a preceding direct object, feminine or masculine depending on the noun, and the participle would agree accordingly.)


That edge case trips up learners because it sits at the intersection of pronoun placement and agreement rules, two things that are usually taught far apart. Parrot's Comprehensible Input Method sequences exposure so learners encounter these constructions in context through its short-form video feed before being asked to produce them, learning without it feeling like studying.


### Passé Composé in Full - Conjugating Vendre Across All Six Persons


-


**je** → j'ai vendu.


-


**tu** → tu as vendu.


-


**il/elle/on** → il a vendu.


-


**nous** → nous avons vendu.


-


**vous** → vous avez vendu.


-


**ils/elles** → ils ont vendu.


Agreement rules for past participles with avoir only apply in specific pronoun constructions, a[direct-object pronoun](https://www.lawlessfrench.com/grammar/direct-object-pronouns/) placed *before* the verb, not in the standard subject-verb-object sentence most learners use first. That distinction matters when comparing sentences like *j'ai vendu la voiture* and *je la vendais chaque été* , the first is passé composé because the sale happened once and finished. Choosing between *j'ai vendu* and *je vendais* under time pressure in actual speech is the second, harder layer, and drilling the table alone does not build that skill.


## How to Conjugate RE Verbs in the Future and Conditional Tenses Without Extra Memorization


That is the whole trick for RE verbs in the future and conditional, and once it clicks, a category of written errors simply disappears. Many learners treat the future and conditional as separate mountains: two sets of endings, two memorization sessions, two chances to confuse "vendrai" with "vendrais" mid-sentence. Both tenses build from the same stem, which means the spelling work you do once carries over automatically.


### One Stem Two Tenses How Dropping the Final E Unlocks Both Future and Conditional


That single step produces the *vendr-* stem that powers both tenses. What most language researchers consistently find is that systematic[morphological errors in written French persist](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7386207/) even after learners have studied conjugation charts, because passive memorization of paradigm tables is insufficient for accurate production. For learners who have already spent time staring at conjugation tables without the errors disappearing, this structural reframe is the research-backed alternative that actually moves the needle. The International Journal of Language and Linguistics (IJLI) and work collected in Springer both reinforce that durable morphological acquisition depends on systematic, contextualized exposure, not isolated drills.


### Full Future Tense Table for Vendre and the One Spelling Trap That Trips Up Written French


-


**je** → **vendrai** → I will sell.


-


**tu** → **vendras** → you will sell.


-


**il/elle/on** → **vendra** → he/she/one will sell.


-


**nous** → **vendrons** → we will sell.


-


**vous** → **vendrez** → you will sell.


-


**ils/elles** → **vendront** → they will sell.


The most common written error: keeping the -e before adding the -r ending, producing "vendrEai" instead of "vendrai." Broader patterns across the field confirm that spelling and morphological mistakes in written French are frequent and patterned enough to require systematic classification, not just generic chart review. Dropping the -e is the one fix that eliminates the entire error class. Parrot App's short-form video feed surfaces native-speaker sentences containing these forms in natural speech, so when you encounter *"je vendrai"* as a Parrot Back speaking prompt, you have already heard it in context dozens of times. That same stem-first logic extends directly to the conditional, as the side-by-side table below makes clear.


The stem never changes. Only the suffix shifts, and the conditional endings (-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient) are the same endings used in the imparfait, so there is genuinely nothing new to memorize from scratch. Compare: *"Je vendrai ma voiture l'année prochaine"* (future, decided) versus *"Je vendrais bien ce vélo si tu le voulais"* (conditional, hypothetical). Regular RE verbs follow this pattern reliably, but a handful of high-frequency RE verbs refuse to follow the regular pattern entirely, and those are precisely the ones French speakers reach for most often in conversation, which is exactly what the next section maps out.

## Irregular RE Verbs That Break the Rules and How to Spot Them Fast


Irregular *verbes du troisième groupe* like prendre break the standard stem-plus-ending formula entirely. Learners who rely only on the regular pattern approach these high-frequency verbs with false confidence. One of the most persistent frustrations beginners face is that even after studying a conjugation family carefully, they still cannot reliably predict the conjugated form of a new irregular RE verb when it appears in real content, because stem or stress changes break expected rules in ways that feel genuinely unpredictable. Most of the irregular RE verbs worth knowing cluster into tight families, and cracking one verb in a family hands you the rest for free.


### The Prendre Family - One Irregular Stem, Five Verbs for Free


**Prendre, apprendre, comprendre, surprendre, and reprendre** all share the same irregular conjugation pattern. The stem drops the *-d* in plural forms, and the third-person plural shifts to *ils prennent* instead of a regular ending. Dummies confirms that because apprendre and comprendre are compounds of prendre, mastering prendre's conjugation automatically transfers to the entire family, replacing five separate memorization tasks with one.


When you spot a verb that ends in *-prendre* , you already know its irregular shape, and Parrot's Comprehensible Input Method, which governs how content is selected and sequenced for each learner, surfaces these verbs inside short-form video content at the moment a learner is ready to absorb them. Mettre trips learners in writing because the *je* form is je mets, a single *-t* , not the doubled *-tt* the infinitive suggests. Suivre creates a parallel trap: the stem shrinks to *sui-* in singular forms, so learners who apply regular logic produce wrong endings.


These are predictable written errors that surface whenever a learner extends the infinitive spelling into conjugated forms without checking. The fix is treating each verb's singular stem as its own unit, separate from the infinitive spelling, and confirming it once before writing. If *ils* sounds or looks noticeably different from *je* (as in *je prends* versus *ils prennent* , as Dummies details), the verb is irregular.


If the stem holds steady and the endings follow the regular pattern, you are dealing with a standard verb. That single test sidesteps the need to front-load a master list of every irregular RE verb before you start reading or listening. It also trains a skill that transfers: recognising stem instability is exactly how fluent readers process new verbs in context, and that kind of active pattern recognition is harder to build than simple memorization yet more consequential in real interactions.


## Why Drilling RE Verb Tables Alone Keeps Fluency Just Out of Reach


But the brain that aced the worksheet and the brain that handles live French conversation are not running the same software.


### Why Your Brain Treats a Conjugation Table Differently Than Spoken Speech


*"Learners are taught conjugation as letter-based rules rather than sound-based rules, making 'irregular' patterns feel arbitrary and harder to internalize, a core reason drilling RE verb tables in isolation fails to build fluency."*


— what we hear from language learners / educators


[Neurolinguistic research draws a clear](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8727903/) line between two distinct memory systems:[explicit (declarative) knowledge](https://opentext.uoregon.edu/languagelearningedition1/chapter/procedural-and-declarative-knowledge/) , which is what you build when you memorize a conjugation table, and[implicit (procedural) knowledge](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/studies-in-second-language-acquisition/article/measuring-implicit-and-explicit-linguistic-knowledge/4E6876DB6AE3C801B1A7105886E5ADFE) , which fires automatically when you speak without thinking.[Drilling a chart loads](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/259349628_Declarative_and_procedural_memory_as_individual_differences_in_second_language_acquisition) the first system, but it does not automatically build the second. Most learners are taught conjugation as a system of letter-based rules, add *-ons* , drop the *-re* , swap the stem, rather than as a system of *sound-based* rules.


That letter-first framing is precisely why patterns that deviate from the template feel arbitrary and are so hard to internalize. A learner who has studied *ils vendent* on a page but never heard it at native speed will still process it slowly mid-conversation, because the sound pattern was never encoded implicitly, and fluency requires that procedural layer to be in place.[Research spanning several decades consistently](https://arabicallthetime.com/blog/does-comprehensible-input-work-research) shows that explicit grammar instruction produces only limited, short-term accuracy gains and does not transfer reliably to spontaneous spoken production, a pattern reflected across multiple meta-analyses of second-language acquisition outcomes.


[Stephen Krashen's Input Hypothesis](https://arabicallthetime.com/blog/does-comprehensible-input-work-research) argues that implicit competence builds through repeated exposure to meaningful, understandable language in context, not through rule memorization. Each time your brain processes *il vend* inside a real sentence it understands, it consolidates the form at the procedural level and begins encoding the *sound* of the ending, not just its spelling. Industry research reinforces this directly, arguing that grammatical patterns must be processed within real communicative environments to become neurologically entrenched.


One practical way to create that environment is through tools built around native-speaker input: its short-form video feed of native-speaker content means every session is simultaneously a listening practice session. You are not just reading *vendent* ; you are hearing it embedded in real sentences, at real speed, with video transcripts displayed alongside video content, with inline translation support, so learners can read what they hear and look up unfamiliar words in context without leaving the feed. That kind of repeated, contextual exposure moves a form from the declarative system into the procedural one, which is a reason to pair the rules you have built here with the listening practice that makes those rules stick.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Why does 'il vend' have no ending, is that a typo?


It is not a typo. The zero ending is the rule for regular -RE verbs: the third-person singular form is simply the bare stem, so 'il vend,' 'elle répond,' and 'il attend' are all correct with nothing added. This surprises most learners because -ER verbs always add an -e and -IR verbs always add a -t, so the silence of the -RE pattern feels wrong until the ear adjusts to it.


### How is conjugating -RE verbs different from -ER and -IR verbs?


All three families start by stripping the infinitive ending to get a stem, but what each family adds to the third-person singular is what sets them apart: -ER verbs add -e, -IR verbs add -t, and -RE verbs add nothing at all. That zero ending is the defining structural feature of the -RE family and the main reason the pattern is treated as its own verb group in French.


### Which -RE verb endings are silent when spoken aloud?


Two endings are completely silent in natural speech: the third-person singular (il/elle/on), which has no ending at all, and the third-person plural -ent ending on ils/elles. That means 'il vend' and 'ils vendent' sound identical, and the only signal between them is the subject pronoun, not the verb ending.


### What are some real-sentence examples of -RE verbs in action?


The post pairs every present-tense form of vendre and répondre with an everyday sentence. For vendre: 'Je vends mon vélo' (I'm selling my bike), 'Il vend sa voiture ce week-end' (He's selling his car this weekend), and 'Ils vendent au marché' (They sell at the market). For répondre: 'Tu réponds vite' (You reply quickly) and 'Elle répond sans hésiter' (She answers without hesitating).


### What is the quickest way to form the past tense of a regular -RE verb?


Drop -re from the infinitive and add -u to get the past participle, then pair it with the correct form of avoir. So vendre becomes vendu, perdre becomes perdu, and attendre becomes attendu, the same mechanical swap every time with no spelling exceptions.
